card.name: Alardah Alnajdiyah (Saudi Ardah)
card.tagline: A rhythmic display of tribal strength, swordplay, and chanted poetry from the Najd.
card.profile: Alardah Alnajdiyah is a traditional Saudi performance combining chanted poetry, rhythmic drumming, and synchronized sword movements. Performed by two facing rows of men, it originated as a martial display among the tribes of the Najd region to boost morale before battle. Today, it serves as a central cultural symbol of Saudi Arabia, performed at weddings, national festivals, and state ceremonies to signify group cohesion and respect.
card.insight: Once a pre-war display of tribal combat readiness, this dance is now the kingdom's most televised performance, where even monarchs join the rows to brandish swords.
card.profile_long: Alardah Alnajdiyah is a traditional Saudi performance that integrates chanted poetry, rhythmic drumming, and synchronized dance movements. The practice is performed by two rows of men facing one another, creating a central space for the performance to unfold. Participants, who may be of any age or social background, often carry light swords or canes as they move. The performance is marked by the repetition of verses and songs, which function as a chorus, while the dancers execute rhythmic movements of the body and sword. The drumming follows a specific sequence, starting with larger drums before transitioning to smaller ones. Throughout the performance, participants shift their bodies forward and backward while raising and lowering their swords, often tilting the hand holding the weapon to one side. A central figure, often carrying a flag, serves as a focal point around which the participants gather at the conclusion of the ceremony. Originally a martial display intended to demonstrate the fighting strength of Najdi tribes and boost morale before armed engagements, the dance has evolved into a ubiquitous cultural symbol. It is now performed at a wide range of occasions, including weddings, births, graduations, and national festivals. The practice is considered a fundamental component of the cultural expression of the communities that perform it, emphasizing group cohesion and respect. While historically restricted to men, the role of women in the tradition is primarily focused on the creation of the costumes worn by the performers. The Saudi government has actively promoted the preservation of this tradition, which was inscribed on the UNESCO Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2015.

sections.origins_and_history: The term 'ardah' is believed to derive from the Arabic verb 'ard', meaning 'to show' or 'to parade'. Historically, the dance was performed by men of the Najd region to publicly demonstrate tribal combat strength and elevate morale before entering war. In the 21st century, the Saudi government formally adopted the name 'Saudi Ardah' to distinguish this specific Najdi variant.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance is performed by two rows of men facing each other. Participants move their bodies forward and backward in rhythm with the drums and poetry. Dancers may brandish a sword or cane, raising and lowering it while tilting their hand to one side. A flag-bearer often stands in the center, and the group gathers around them at the end of the performance.
sections.music_and_instruments: The performance is accompanied by rhythmic drumming and chanted poetry. The drumming sequence begins with larger drums, followed by smaller ones. The poetry, which relates to the specific event being celebrated, is recited by a poet and repeated by the participants as a refrain.
sections.costume_and_setting: Performers wear traditional costumes and carry light swords or canes. The setting is typically an open space suitable for two rows of men to face each other, often at weddings, national festivals, or state ceremonies.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Alardah Alnajdiyah marks important personal, local, and national occasions, including weddings, births, and graduations. It is a symbol of group cohesion and respect, serving as a vital expression of Saudi cultural identity.
sections.regional_variants: While Najdi Ardah is the most common and televised form in Saudi Arabia, other variations exist throughout the Arabian Peninsula. Within Saudi Arabia, distinct regional versions are practiced in the southern provinces of Najran, Asir, and Jizan.
sections.lineage: The dance is part of the broader tradition of Ardah found across the Arabian Peninsula, sharing thematic similarities with other regional performances like the Mizmar and Yowlah.

basic_steps: Form two parallel rows facing each other.
Step forward and backward in rhythm with the drums.
Raise and lower the sword or cane in time with the body movement.
Tilt the hand holding the sword to one side.
